text: By the end of this unit, students will be able to: speak confidently and fluently in a wide range of contexts (conflict resolution, panel discussion, role-play, dialogue) for purposes like exposition and argumentation; analyse that a text comprises paragraphs developing a main idea; apply skimming and scanning strategies to identify writer's purpose and audience, infer the main idea, and distinguish fact from opinion; examine the central idea of an informational text and its relationship to supporting ideas, and provide an objective summary; demonstrate knowledge of parts of speech in oral and written communication; follow the process approach to plan a paragraph (brainstorming, structuring, mind-mapping, free writing, note-taking); write informative/explanatory texts that convey complex ideas clearly.

Arabia is a land of unparalleled charm and beauty, with sand dunes under a tropical sun; the Rasoolullah (SAW) was born in Makkah, about fifty miles from the Red Sea. The Arabs had remarkable memory and eloquence, expressed through poetry; a yearly poetic fair was held at Ukaz. In the fifth and sixth centuries, mankind stood on the verge of chaos, and Allah raised a Rasool to lift humanity from ignorance into the light of faith. At the age of thirty-eight, the Rasoolullah (SAW) spent much time in solitude and meditation in the cave of Hira. His heart was filled with compassion for humanity and an urge to eradicate wrong beliefs, cruelty and injustice. Hazrat Jibril (AS) conveyed the first revelation: 'Read in the name of thy Lord Who created...' (Quran, 96:1-5). The revelation continued for twenty-three years; the Rasoolullah's (SAW) mission was to proclaim the Oneness of Allah (Tauheed) and the unity of mankind, destroying the nexus of superstition and disbelief. As the pagan Arabs felt threatened, they pressured the Rasoolullah (SAW) and his followers to renounce their cause, even approaching his uncle Hazrat Abu Talib. The Rasoolullah (SAW) famously replied that even if they placed the sun in his right hand and the moon in his left, he would not abandon the proclamation of Tauheed. Abu Talib, moved by his nephew's determination, promised never to forsake him. The Rasoolullah (SAW) is universally acknowledged as the most influential figure in history; historian Michael H. Hart credited him with shaping both the theology and ethical principles of Islam and driving the Arab conquests. Hazrat Ayesha (RA) said his morals and character were an embodiment of the Holy Quran. Quran 33:45-46 describes him as a witness, a bearer of good news, a warner, and a light-giving torch.

bestow: to give something as an honour or gift. chaos: lack of order, disorder. compassion: sympathy. crumble: to break into very small pieces. dazzling: so bright you cannot see for a short time. dilemma: a situation that makes problems. dispensation: special permission to do something. dune: a small hill of sand. eloquence: the ability to use language and express opinions well. embodiment: a typical example of an idea or quality. eradicate: to destroy or get rid of something. everlasting: continuing forever. meditation: focusing the mind in silence, especially to make it calm. nexus: a complicated series of connections between things. proclaim: to publicly and officially tell people about something important. promulgation: the act of spreading an idea or belief among many people. proselytizing: trying to persuade other people to accept your beliefs. renounce: to state publicly that you no longer hold a belief or will behave in a particular way. solitude: the state of being alone, especially when pleasant. theology: the study of religions and beliefs. transformation: a complete change in somebody or something. tropical: the hottest area between the two tropics. unparalleled: bigger or better than anything else like it. verge: the edge of a path or road.

Comprehension questions on Unit 1: how the geographical description of Makkah influences understanding of its importance; what the Arabs' memory and eloquence suggest about pre-Islamic culture; the significance of the Hammad/Caliph Walid anecdote; parallels between the described decline/renewal and other historical periods; challenges the Rasoolullah (SAW) faced in proclaiming Tauheed and unity; how he elevated mankind spiritually and worldly; how the final Quranic verse (33:45-46) encapsulates his role and mission; the author's view of pre-Islamic Arabs with supporting evidence.

Word change example, base word 'Analyze': Verb - Analyze (to examine methodically); Noun - Analysis (the process of examining); Adjective - Analytical (relating to analysis); Adverb - Analytically (in a manner using logical reasoning). A prefix is added to the beginning of a word to change its meaning, e.g. 're-' + 'write' = 'rewrite' (to write again). A suffix is added to the end of a word to change its form or meaning, e.g. '-er' + 'teach' = 'teacher' (someone who teaches).

Noun: names a person, place, thing, or idea (teacher, city, book, happiness). Pronoun: replaces a noun - personal (I, you, he, she, it, we, they), possessive (mine, yours, his, hers, ours, theirs), reflexive (myself, yourself, himself...), demonstrative (this, that, these, those), interrogative (who, whom, whose, which, what), relative (who, whom, whose, which, that). Verb: expresses action or state of being - action verbs (run, jump, write), linking verbs (am, is, are, was, were, be), helping verbs (have, has, had, do, does, did). Adjective: describes a noun or pronoun - qualitative (happy, blue, tall), quantitative (some, many, few), demonstrative (this, that), possessive (my, your, his). Adverb: modifies a verb, adjective, or another adverb, showing how/when/where/to what extent (quickly, now, here, very). Preposition: shows relationship between a noun/pronoun and other words (in, on, at, by, with, under, over, between, among). Conjunction: connects words, phrases, or clauses - coordinating (and, but, or, nor, for, so, yet), subordinating (because, although, since, unless, while), correlative (either...or, neither...nor, both...and). Interjection: expresses strong emotion or surprise (wow, oh, ouch, hooray, alas).

By the end of this unit, students will be able to: respond to text through oral discussion, telling short stories, and acting plays; read with correct pronunciation, pitch, and voice variation for fictional and nonfictional texts; distinguish cause from effect and fact from opinion, and generalized statements from evidence-based information; read and analyse expositions such as reviews and arguments; apply parts of speech, tenses, and sentence structure to understand how language functions; write arguments to support claims using valid reasoning and sufficient evidence.

Patriotism means love for the motherland or devotion to one's country; the word 'patriot' comes from the Latin 'patriota', meaning countryman, and is a commendable quality. Patriotism gives people strength and courage to safeguard the country's interests; sovereignty, integrity, and honour are supreme values on which no compromise can be made, and patriots render great sacrifice to preserve them. Quaid-e-Azam Muhammad Ali Jinnah was a nation builder and great patriot who protected the values, culture, and traditions of the Muslims of the subcontinent and secured a separate homeland for them, saying: 'We must develop a sense of patriotism which galvanizes us all into a united and strong nation.' The spirit of patriotism keeps a nation alert against foreign invasion. In the wars of 1965, 1971, and the Kargil War 1999, many brave soldiers laid down their lives, including Naik Saif Ali Janjua Shaheed, Captain Muhammad Sarwar Shaheed, Major Tufail Muhammad Shaheed, Major Raja Aziz Bhatti Shaheed, Pilot Officer Rashid Minhas Shaheed, Major Shabbir Sharif Shaheed, Sowar Muhammad Hussain Shaheed, Major Muhammad Akram Shaheed, Lance Naik Muhammad Mahfuz Shaheed, Havildar Lalak Jan Shaheed, and Captain Karnal Sher Khan Shaheed - all awarded Nishan-e-Haider, Pakistan's highest military award. Patriotism is not just a feeling but a live spirit that inspires and guides a nation; S.W. Scott wrote that a man devoid of patriotic spirit is like one who 'Breathes there the man, with soul so dead, Who never to himself hath said, This is my own, my native land!'

commendable: deserving praise and approval. devoid: completely without something, deprived. devotion: great love, care and support for somebody/something. embrace: accepting an idea, proposal or belief with enthusiasm. instances: examples. martyrdom: the suffering of death for adherence to a cause, especially religious or political faith. native: connected with the place where you were born and lived early in life. preservation: keeping something in its original or good condition. spirit: a person's feelings or state of mind. supreme: highest in rank or position.

Exercises distinguishing cause from effect (e.g. patriots render sacrifice for the preservation of the country's values; during the wars of 1965 and 1971 many soldiers displayed great courage) and fact from opinion (e.g. 'Patriotism is a commendable quality' is an opinion; 'Many soldiers were awarded Nishan-e-Haider for their bravery' is a fact), as well as distinguishing generalized statements from evidence-based information.

Simple Present: habitual actions/general truths, e.g. 'She writes in her journal every day.' Simple Past: actions completed at a specific past time, e.g. 'He visited the museum last weekend.' Simple Future: actions at a specific future time, e.g. 'They will travel to Quetta next summer.' Present Continuous: actions happening now, e.g. 'She is reading a book.' Past Continuous: ongoing past actions, e.g. 'He was cooking dinner when the phone rang.' Future Continuous: actions ongoing in the future, e.g. 'They will be waiting for us at the airport.' Present Perfect: actions at an unspecified past time or continuing to the present, e.g. 'She has lived here for ten years.' Past Perfect: actions completed before another past action, e.g. 'They had finished their homework before dinner.' Future Perfect: actions completed before a specific future time, e.g. 'She will have graduated by next year.' Present Perfect Continuous: actions started in the past, still continuing, e.g. 'She has been studying for three hours.' Past Perfect Continuous: ongoing past actions before another past action, e.g. 'He had been working there for five years before he left.' Future Perfect Continuous: actions continuing up to a specific future time, e.g. 'By next month, she will have been working here for a year.'

A gerund is the -ing form of a verb functioning as a noun (subject: 'Swimming is fun'; object of a verb: 'She enjoys reading'; after prepositions: 'They talked about going on holiday'; after certain verbs: 'He suggested meeting earlier'). An infinitive is 'to' + base verb (subject: 'To err is human'; object of a verb: 'He wants to learn French'; after adjectives: 'She is eager to start'; to express purpose: 'I went to the store to buy milk'). Certain verbs change meaning with gerund vs infinitive: remember + -ing (recalling a past event) vs remember + to (not forgetting a future task); stop + -ing (ceasing an activity) vs stop + to (pausing to do something else); try + -ing (experimenting) vs try + to (making an effort); forget + -ing vs forget + to; regret + -ing vs regret + to; go on + -ing (continuing) vs go on + to (moving to something new). Participles are verb forms used as adjectives: present participles (-ing, e.g. 'the running water') and past participles (-ed/-en, e.g. 'the broken vase'), also used in continuous/perfect tenses, passive voice, and participial phrases (e.g. 'Running down the street, he met an old friend').

By the end of this unit, students will be able to: demonstrate attentive listening skills with standard pronunciation and intonation; use pre-reading and while-reading strategies to explore layers of meaning including biases and opinions; understand figurative language, word relationships, and nuances in word meanings; identify and use compound prepositions and prepositional phrases; paraphrase a poem; write an objective summary of a given text or poem.

I wandered lonely as a cloud / That floats on high o'er vales and hills, / When all at once I saw a crowd, / A host of golden daffodils; / Beside the lake, beneath the trees, / Fluttering and dancing in the breeze. Continuous as the stars that shine / And twinkle on the milky way, / They stretched in never-ending line / Along the margin of a bay: / Ten thousand saw I at a glance / Tossing their heads in sprightly dance. The waves beside them danced, but they / Out-did the sparkling waves in glee: / A poet could not but be gay, / In such a jocund company! / I gazed - and gazed - but little thought / What wealth the show to me had brought. For oft, when on my couch I lie / In vacant or in pensive mood, / They flash upon that inward eye / Which is the bliss of solitude; / And then my heart with pleasure fills / And dances with the daffodils. 'Daffodils' was inspired by a walk William Wordsworth (1770-1850) took with his sister Dorothy near Ullswater in the Lake District on April 15, 1802.

The theme of 'Daffodils' includes: the beauty of nature (celebrating the daffodils' vibrant, joyful presence); the power of memory (how memories of beautiful natural experiences bring lasting comfort and happiness); solitude and connection (the poet's initial loneliness transforms into joyful connection with nature); emotional and spiritual uplift (nature elevates the poet's mood and spirit). Other Wordsworth poems: To the Cuckoo, Lucy Grey, The World is too Much with Us, The Two April Mornings, It is a Beauteous Evening, Solitary Reaper, We are Seven.

bliss: happiness. continuous: spreading in a line without spaces. fluttering: moving lightly and quickly. host: a large number of people or things. jocund: cheerful. milky way: the band of stars across the night sky including our sun and its planets. pensive: thinking deeply. solitude: the state of being alone. sprightly: full of life and energy. vacant: empty or unoccupied. vales: valleys. wandered: to walk slowly around.

Denotation is the literal, dictionary meaning of a word; connotation is the ideas or feelings a word invokes beyond its literal meaning. Example: 'Lonely' (denotative: being without company) carries a negative connotation implying sadness and abandonment, while 'Solitary' (denotative: existing alone) carries a neutral/positive connotation suggesting peacefulness and deliberate choice. Nuance refers to subtle differences in meaning, tone, or feeling between similar words. Word relationships include synonyms, antonyms, homophones, homonyms, and analogies.

Simile: compares two different things using 'like' or 'as', e.g. 'I wandered lonely as a cloud' (compares loneliness to a drifting cloud). Personification: gives human qualities to non-human things, e.g. 'Fluttering and dancing in the breeze' (daffodils described as dancing). Hyperbole: an exaggerated statement for emphasis, e.g. 'Ten thousand saw I at a glance.' Metaphor: directly refers to one thing by naming another, e.g. 'They flash upon that inward eye' (memory/imagination as an 'inward eye'). Alliteration: repetition of the same consonant sound at the start of nearby words, e.g. 'Beside the lake, beneath the trees.' Assonance: repetition of vowel sounds in nearby words, e.g. 'A host of golden daffodils.' Imagery: descriptive language appealing to the senses, e.g. 'Continuous as the stars that shine / And twinkle on the milky way.'

A euphemism is a mild or indirect word/expression substituted for something harsher or unpleasant, e.g. 'passed away' instead of 'died', 'let go' instead of 'fired', 'senior citizen' instead of 'old person'; used to soften unpleasant information. An oxymoron combines contradictory words with opposite meanings, e.g. 'bitter sweets', 'deafening silence', 'jumbo shrimp'; used to create dramatic effect or highlight complexity through contrast. 'Daffodils' contains neither device, since Wordsworth's language is direct and aims for a harmonious, uplifting tone.

Compound prepositions are multi-word phrases functioning as a single preposition: 'according to' (as stated by) - 'According to the teacher, the test will be held next week'; 'due to' (because of) - 'The match was cancelled due to heavy rain'; 'in front of' (before/ahead of) - 'The car is parked in front of the house'; 'on behalf of' (representing someone) - 'She accepted the award on behalf of her team'; 'in addition to' (along with) - 'In addition to his studies, he also plays football'; 'in spite of' (despite) - 'In spite of the cold weather, they went for a walk.'

A prepositional phrase = preposition + object of the preposition, giving information about time (before, during), location (in, on), direction (to, towards), cause (because of, due to), manner (with a smile, by hand), or condition (in case of, in the event of). It can function as an adjective phrase (describing a noun, e.g. 'The book on the shelf is interesting') or an adverb phrase (describing a verb/adjective/adverb, e.g. 'She sang with joy'). Common errors: misplaced prepositional phrases that confuse meaning, and overusing too many phrases in one sentence.

topic: Writing Skills: Paraphrasing and Summary Writing
text: Paraphrasing means re-writing a poet's expressions or ideas in one's own words without changing the original meaning, keeping roughly the same length. Summary writing follows four steps: (1) Reading - thoroughly read and understand the original text, noting main ideas, themes, and significant details; (2) Outlining - note the author's purpose, main topic sentence, key supporting details, and central idea; (3) Drafting - combine notes into coherent sentences and paragraphs, keeping it brief and free of personal opinions; (4) Reviewing - check for accuracy, completeness, and clarity, refining the language.
